evidence: "# 1. bipartition"; the other solutions build "components" with two color partitions
affordance_in_statement: The system's physical constraints guarantee that destructive resonance is only possible between two modules if the difference between their frequency bands is an odd integer.
removal_suggestion: Remove the odd-difference frequency guarantee, or replace it with an unrestricted frequency-difference rule. This preserves the numeric bounds, input format, output format, and examples while preventing the conflict graph from being guaranteed bipartite.

survivor_shortcuts.shortcut: Recognizes that the conflict graph is bipartite and begins with a bipartition-based algorithm, enabling a matching/vertex-cover solution for the independent-set witness.
survivor_shortcuts.affordance: The system's physical constraints guarantee that destructive resonance is only possible ... if the difference between their frequency bands is an odd integer.

common_affordance: The conflict graph is guaranteed to be bipartite because every reported edge joins modules whose hidden integer frequencies have opposite parity.

defeated_student_causes.why_failed: It partitions each connected component into two color classes and treats selecting an entire side per component as sufficient. A maximum independent set in a bipartite component can mix vertices from both sides, so this misses valid configurations.

Its partition-based construction makes the same invalid whole-color-class assumption rather than computing a general maximum independent set via matching/vertex cover; mixed-side independent sets can be larger.
It similarly stores bipartite component partitions and restricts the candidate solution to those partitions, which is not sufficient for maximum independent set in a general bipartite graph.

recommended_edit: Change the sentence imposing the odd frequency-difference restriction to state that resonance pairs may have arbitrary integer frequency differences, with no parity guarantee.
